item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers will activate Dalton Rushing on Friday before their final regular-season series, giving the left-handed power hitter at least a few more days and a handful of at-bats to unleash his swing.
The Dodgers are not ruling out a possible spot on a playoff roster, but as of now, they are just focused on giving Rushing the chance to take a few swings in San Francisco in a sign of respect.
“At the most it would be three pinch-hit at-bats, so just conduct at-bats and see what you got,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “Just the circumstances of his situation, it’s just tough to just be hurt, come back, then be hurt again, and then take three pinch-hit at-bats to potentially then say, ‘Hey, you’re on the roster.’
“What he’s done for us this season certainly deserves some (playoff) consideration. That’s kind of giving him the respect and thoughtfulness of what he’s done for us.”
Rushing understands the situation and is fully on board with whatever decision is made.
His season was put in jeopardy when he went on the injured list in early August with an elbow injury that was diagnosed as a small UCL tear with a forearm flexor strain.
Determined to return as both a hitter and a catcher, Rushing worked at both sides of his game and returned on Sept. 1. But the continued throwing work outside of games led to a setback and he went back on the IL less than a week later.
“The at-bat’s really are the only side that I can truly help them in,” Rushing said Thursday. “Even then, it’s just a pinch-hit opportunity and no defense included, so I know that ties their hands up a little bit. But yeah, I’m excited.”
Without much time to make an impact, and the Dodgers also having the option of using left-handed-hitting rookie Josue De Paula on the playoff roster, Rushing is well aware of what he is up against. The club even has the option of using the lefty hitting Hyeseong Kim in the playoffs for his defense and speed.
“No hard feelings on either end,” Rushing said about getting a chance to play in the playoffs. “Obviously you want to play baseball. You feel healthy again to an extent. You feel healthy swinging a bat, so yeah, I want to get back soon.”
The next challenge is determining the extent of his elbow injury. Rushing is swinging pain-free after a platelet-rich plasma injection, but figuring out when he can throw again remains in question.
He is determined to rehab the injury, knowing that some kind of surgical procedure might be needed.
“I think as soon as we get into the offseason, that’s decision time,” Rushing said. “Progressing the way that I’m progressing right now, I’m very optimistic it is going to be totally fine and just think it was a lot of workload increase very quickly. I think that’s what sparked it. Once I got the shot, it felt really, really good.”
Roberts did not say what the full roster move will be on Friday.
VIEW FROM THE TOP
Shohei Ohtani was back in the leadoff spot on Thursday after batting second in his return from the IL on Wednesday.
While his turn as a No. 2 hitter came because the San Diego Padres had left-hander Robbie Ray on the mound, Roberts has not said if batting second against a lefty will be a regular feature of the lineup.
“I’m kind of toying with it clearly,” Roberts said. “But I’m not sure exactly whether he’s going to stick in the one or rotate him depending on the pitcher.”
Ohtani went 1 for 4 with a walk on Wednesday, but the comfort level he showed at the plate pleased Roberts.
“I hope that’s a sign of things to come,” Roberts said. “Taking the first slider from Robbie Ray for a ball, (that) got him into a good count, whereas the last couple weeks he was just hair-on-fire swinging and chasing. It’s a hard way to make a living that way, right? I thought (Wednesday) the patience was really good. I hope that’s more to come.”
CATCHING ON FAST
After starting the first two games of the series against the Padres, catcher Will Smith gave way to backup Hunter Feduccia on Thursday but was available off the bench.
Smith is also set to start two of the three games in San Francisco over the weekend before settling into an everyday role in the playoffs.
In the last five games Smith started, he was batting .421 (8 for 19) with three home runs and five RBIs. Since returning from neck inflammation on Sept. 1, he is batting .255 with four home runs and 11 RBIs in 19 games.
UP NEXT
Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 11-7, 2.85 ERA) at Giants (RHP Yunior Marte, 0-1, 4.66 ERA), Friday, 7:15 p.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM, 1020 AM

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres are facing off in the rubber match of their three-game series on Thursday night with plenty at stake for both teams.
The Dodgers, who have already won the National League West division, can clinch a first-round bye with a win or Atlanta Braves loss over the season's final four games.
They're also still chasing the Milwaukee Brewers for the No. 1 seed, but will need some help to secure home-field advantage throughout the postseason.
As for the Padres, they're looking to clinch a postseason spot, with their magic number currently sitting at 1.
Thus, the winner of Thursday's game will be celebrating in some capacity. If it's the Padres, they'll be making a champagne and beer mess in the visitor's clubhouse at Dodger Stadium. If it's the Dodgers, they'll be shaking hands and looking forward to their five-day layoff beginning next week.
Dodgers vs Padres Pitching Matchup on Thursday
Right-handed pitcher Tyler Glasnow is taking the mound for the Dodgers in his final tune-up before the postseason.
Glasnow has been shaky since coming off the injured list at the end of August, sporting a 4.50 ERA over 28 innings with 38 strikeouts to 10 walks. Overall this season, he's 5-1 with a 3.46 ERA and 87 strikeouts across 67.2 innings (12 starts).
Glasnow is expected to be the team's No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
Opposite Glasnow will be Padres right-hander Nick Pivetta, who missed nearly five months this season with an elbow injury but has been incredibly sharp since returning.
In his three starts since coming off the IL, Pivetta has allowed just three runs over 14 innings for a 1.93 ERA. He has 11 strikeouts to one walk in that time.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers activated Andy Pages from the 10-day injured list and optioned Eliezer Alfonzo to Triple-A Oklahoma City. The move was made during the off day on Monday, but the Dodgers did not officially announce it at the time.
In addition, Roki Sasaki was also activated while Emmet Sheehan was optioned.
The Dodgers first recalled Alfonzo when Dalton Rushing was placed on the IL on Sept. 6. During his second stint with the club, Alfonzo only received one at-bat, which came against the Cincinnati Reds on Sept. 9 when he struck out.
Alfonzo was the third catcher on the roster, which Dodgers manager Dave Roberts explained was to allow the club to more freely use Will Smith and Hunter Feduccia as pinch-hitters when they didn’t start.
The Dodgers also did not need to make a 40-man roster move to call up Alfonzo, which likely played into their decision.
The 26-year-old has appeared in 13 total games this season, making his MLB debut and batting .179/.179/.250 with four RBI and three runs scored in 28 plate appearances. In Oklahoma City, he was hitting .302/.378/.409 in 256 plate appearances.
Pages is back with the Dodgers for the first time in a month after he landed on the IL with a left hand fracture on Aug. 22.
Pages suffered the injury when he was hit by a pitch from Pittsburgh Pirates starter Bubba Chandler. The 26-year-old underwent surgery shortly after to insert a compression screw in his hand to speed up the healing process.
Pages did not go on a rehab assignment before returning, but did workouts at Dodger Stadium, which included hitting on the field, running the bases, and doing outfield drills.
That makes this stretch of six games important for Pages to face live pitching and get as many at-bats as possible to prepare for the postseason. But even with that in mind, the Dodgers also have to be cautious about building him back up and not overworking him after a month of not playing.
“So we have obviously, assuming he gets back on Tuesday, then there’s six in a row, and that seems pretty aggressive,” Roberts explained.
“So I think that we do want to get him as many at-bats as possible, but we have to make sure that his legs are under him, feeling good, so we don’t go backward or get injured in that respect. So it is going to be a balancing act, and just keeping a keen eye on Andy for sure.”
Pages is batting .272/.338/.458 with 25 doubles, 21 home runs, 80 RBI and 72 runs scored this season. He has also been among the top defensive players in MLB.

item.content:encoded:
Entering the final week of the regular season, the Dodgers more or less know their postseason fate.
They've locked up the National League West. They are a seemingly safe four games clear of the Atlanta Braves for a first-round bye. And, unless they can close a two-game gap on the Milwaukee Brewers without holding the tiebreaker, they will finish as the NL's No. 2 seed, getting home-field advantage at least for the NL Division Series.
Thus, the real intrigue for now is who might be on the Dodgers' postseason roster when the playoffs begin next month.
This year, injuries and fluctuating performances have forced them to cycle 53 different players through their clubhouse.
And while the core of the group is clear, many questions remain about how the club will construct its lineup and pitching staff for this fall's pursuit of a third-straight World Series.
Here is the California Post's best guess about how it will all shake out.
Lineup locks
Will Smith, Freddie Freeman, Tommy Edman, Mookie Betts, Max Muncy, Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Shohei Ohtani, Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Hunter Feduccia
There won't be any big surprises in how the Dodgers line up to begin the playoffs, assuming Ohtani is healthy enough to resume everyday DH'ing duties.
Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker have cemented their place as everyday hitters thanks to late-season surges. Andy Pages is due back on Tuesday from a fractured hand. Freddie Freeman still seems somewhat limited by his right knee injury, but has nonetheless been able to manage it well enough to this point. And while Tommy Edman has been slumping lately, he doesn't seem to be in immediate danger of losing at-bats.
On the bench, Hunter Feduccia has locked up the back-up catching job, and could be a left-handed hitting option as a pinch-hitter. Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, meanwhile, each provide versatile defensive depth, as well as extensive track records for postseason heroics when called upon.
Entering the final week of the regular season, the core of the Dodgers' position player group looks as they expected.
Dodgers Lineup questions
Bubble candidates: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, Alex Freeland, Hyeseong Kim
The Dodgers will still have one, if not two, position player spots to fill depending on how they construct their roster (i.e. an even 13 pitchers/13 hitters, or a 12/14 split like they used last year?)
And for those, they could have a number of difficult decisions.
First and foremost: Will Josue De Paula make the playoff roster?
If he does, it will likely be as a left-handed bench bat; though if there is any lingering uncertainty with Ohtani, he could also provide insurance as a backup DH option. His main competition right now figures to be Alex Call (who might be redundant to Rojas and Hernández as a right-handed bench bat) or Dalton Rushing (who is an intriguing alternative as a left-handed bat, but remains sidelined from the setback he suffered with his elbow injury earlier this month).
In just 10 MLB games, De Paula has quickly built a strong case, showing supreme plate discipline (10 walks to only four strikeouts) and the potential for power (three doubles, one home run, seven RBIs). At this point, it might be more of a surprise if he doesn't make it.
If the Dodgers elect to carry an extra position player on top of that, the choices are even more varied.
Last year, they rostered two base-running/defensive specialists throughout the playoffs in infielder Hyeseong Kim and outfielder Justin Dean. Dean is now gone, and Hernández could serve as a late-game defensive outfield replacement anyway. But Kim remains in consideration, manager Dave Roberts said, thanks to his speed and infield glove. Alex Freeland could also factor in here, as someone capable of providing more at the plate.
Lineup projection for Los Angeles
C: Will Smith
1B: Freddie Freeman
2B: Tommy Edman
SS: Mookie Betts
3B: Max Muncy
LF: Teoscar Hernández
CF: Andy Pages
RF: Kyle Tucker
DH: Shohei Ohtani
Bench: Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Hunter Feduccia, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim*
*If the Dodgers carry 14 position players
Dodgers pitching staff locks
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Roki Sasaki, Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips
The Dodgers' starting rotation is set, assuming no further setbacks with Blake Snell's groin injury. The back end of the bullpen has come into focus, too, with Tanner Scott and/or Roki Sasaki the most logical candidates to serve as closer, and Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips separating themselves as the team's next most-trusted high-leverage relief options.
The only real question here is how the Dodgers will line up the rotation. Yamamoto-Skubal would make sense for Games 1 and 2 of a division series (keeping them both on-line for a potential Game 5). But could Tyler Glasnow's potential issues with traveling tempt the Dodgers to use him primarily at home, if they can? All factors to consider in the coming weeks.
Pitching staff questions
Roster bubble candidates: Brock Stewart, Edwin Díaz, Blake Treinen, Kris Bubic, Jack Dreyer, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski, Edgardo Henriquez, Will Klein, Eric Lauer
The first thing the Dodgers need to figure out here is health.
Edgardo Henriquez will almost certainly be on the playoff roster, and pitching in a high-leverage role, if he can make a full recovery from his recent back strain. Will Klein and Eric Lauer might also be available health-wise, though lack clear roles to step immediately back into.
Otherwise, the Dodgers will effectively have at least four open spots for six to seven other pitchers.
For added right-handed depth, they might be deciding between Brock Stewart (who has been a go-to weapon against right-handed hitters recently), Edwin Díaz (who is trying to salvage his dismal debut season, and did throw a pair of scoreless outings this weekend) and Blake Treinen (who has curiously pitched only five times in three weeks since being activated from the injured list, and not in the highest of leverage).
For another left-handed option, they could go with Kris Bubic (the trade deadline acquisition who has impressed with three scoreless appearances since returning from an injury) or Jack Dreyer (who was one of the Dodgers' best relievers from June to August, but has given up five runs in his last seven outings).
And for a multi-inning role, they will have Emmet Sheehan (who has looked like a different pitcher in three sterling starts since returning from a minor-league demotion) and Justin Wrobleski (the breakout All-Star who has finally shaken some of his home run problems since moving to the bullpen).
There are many permutations that the Dodgers could employ depending on opponent. They're still figuring out the exact hierarchy of all their bullpen arms, too.
But as long as their rotation is dominant, everything else should take care of itself.
Pitching staff projection
Rotation: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Bullpen: Roki Sasaki, Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Kris Bubic, Edwin Díaz, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Dave Roberts has a dilemma.
His first baseman, Freddie Freeman, just turned 37 years old and has been slumping badly down the stretch while playing through patellar tendinitis in his right knee. Never one to accept days off as the answer to anything, Freeman would probably benefit from some downtime this week – but he also needs at-bats to rediscover the swing that had him batting .300 for the season just two weeks ago or recalibrate it to accommodate his balky knee.
“There’s rest, but there’s also trying to find your swing,” Roberts acknowledged after putting Freeman in the lineup on Saturday and Sunday – a day game following a night game.
“I think it’s a work in progress,” Roberts said of Freeman’s swing. “The other day in Cincinnati (a three-hit game on Tuesday), I think it was looking pretty good, and then. I actually thought yesterday there were a couple good swings there.
“Obviously, the results weren’t there for him, and he’s frustrated, and I think that you just kind of have to count on him to figure it out and bet on him. And that’s kind of where we’re at. But again, having the week off (with a first-round bye) would be huge too.”
Freeman said he has been doing some different drills in the batting cage, focused on hitting the ball “out front” more.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep, and it caused me to slide,” Freeman said earlier this week. “So today (in the cage) was – foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit.”
Even with that three-hit game in Cincinnati and a two-hit game on Thursday, Freeman went into Sunday just 6 for his past 48 (.125), hitless in nine at-bats in the first two games of the series with the Giants.
“Got to go for results-based things right now,” Freeman said. “Looking to be hot for a few weeks. That’s all I’m trying to do.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results. We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago (when his ankle was injured), I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable. I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
OHTANI WORK
The “hope” is that Shohei Ohtani will be ready to come off the injured list when he is eligible on Wednesday, Roberts said. When he does, Roberts expects him to be in the lineup for the final five games.
“Absolutely,” Roberts said. “Yeah, he’ll need those live at-bats.”
Roberts has said Ohtani is “pain-free” but he acknowledged that Ohtani won’t be feeling 100% when he returns – but will be closer to it than he has been in weeks.
“Discomfort you can play through,” Roberts said of how Ohtani is feeling. “I think there’s a difference between discomfort and pain. Is it 100%? Probably not. Is it better than it was a week ago? Yes.
“Honestly I think that’s just a better question for Shohei to give more specifics, but I do think that when he’s activated it’s going to be the best physical place he’s been in in quite some time.”
Ohtani has spoken with the media just once in the past five weeks (before he went on the IL).
KIM CALL
Signed to a three-year, $12.5 million contract, South Korean infielder Hyeseong Kim has spent most of the second season of that contract in Triple-A where he hit .265 with a .682 OPS in 84 games. He hasn’t been up with the Dodgers since May but Roberts said Kim will be part of the “conversation” for the postseason roster.
“My expectation is Hyeseong will be here during the off week (next week) and potentially be a conversation for the postseason (roster) because he has the ability to run, to play defense, and steal a base,” Roberts said. “He’s in the conversation, yes.”
Kim was on the postseason roster last fall, appearing in just two games. It will be difficult to give him a spot on a bench that seems set with Alex Call, Hunter Feduccia, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernandez and Josue De Paula.
ROSTER MOVES
The Dodgers placed pitcher Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list on Sunday and recalled Emmet Sheehan from Triple-A to pitch ‘bulk’ in Sunday’s game.
Also, reliever Seth Halvorsen was returned to Triple-A and reliever Kyle Hurt was recalled.
Sheehan is still under consideration for a bullpen role on the postseason roster.
UP NEXT
The Dodgers are off on Monday.
Padres (TBA) at Dodgers (TBA), Tuesday, 7:10 p.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers kept right fielder Kyle Tucker out of their lineup for Sunday’s game after he exited Saturday’s win early.
Tucker fouled a ball off of his shin Saturday, and left the game shortly after. Manager Dave Roberts expected Tucker to return to the lineup Sunday, but the outfielder clearly isn’t fit to participate.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
The Dodgers are running a bullpen day on Sunday, and could have a few players fill in if needed. Jack Dreyer is getting the ball first for the Dodgers, making his second start of the season. He has a 3.19 ERA through 63 appearances with 68 strikeouts in 59.1 innings pitched.
Emmet Sheehan has a locker at Dodger Stadium as well, and could handle bulk for LA on Sunday.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
Shortstop Mookie Betts remains in the leadoff spot for the Dodgers, and center fielder Tommy Edman shoots up the order to bat second. Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez bats third, and first baseman Freddie Freeman serves as the cleanup hitter.
Miguel Rojas enters the lineup as the second baseman and No. 5 hitter, and third baseman Max Muncy slides down the order to the No. 6 spot. Josue De Paula remains the team’s designated hitter, and following him are left fielder Kiké Hernandez and catcher Hunter Feduccia to round out the Dodgers’ lineup.
Dodgers Lineup vs. Giants
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Tommy Edman, CF
3. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
4. Freddie Freeman, 1B
5. Miguel Rojas, 2B
6. Max Muncy, 3B
7. Josue De Paula, DH
8. Kiké Hernandez, LF
9. Hunter Feduccia, C
Who is Starting for the Giants?
On the mound for the Giants is left-hander Matt WIlkinson, who will be making his seventh appearance of the year. He has a 4.58 ERA through 19.2 innings pitched, striking out 12 batters durign that time.
The rookie struggled in his first stint as a starter, transitioning to relief for his last two appearances and holding his opponents scoreless.
The Dodgers will look to break his scoreless streak in Sunday’s game, which begins at 1:10 p.m. PT.

item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers brought third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Josue De Paula back into the lineup for Thursday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
The Dodgers lost Wednesday’s game after Cy Young winner Blake Snell went down with a groin injury after pitching just one inning. Luckily, Snell believes he can still make a start before the end of the regular season, which ends in less than two weeks.
LA won the first two games of the series, shutting down a powerful Reds lineup, and will look to do the same to win the series Wednesday.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
Justin Wrobleski will start for the Dodgers on Wednesday, making his 25th appearance of the regular season. Two of his last three appearances have come out of the bullpen, and none of them have lasted more than three innings since his return from the injured list with a forearm problem.
He has a 3.78 ERA on the year, striking out 111 batters over the course of 133.1 innings—his heaviest workload in an MLB season so far.
How deep into the game he goes depends on him, but the Dodgers will have backup in the form of Landon Knack whenever Wrobleski is ready to come out.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers still don’t have Shohei Ohtani in the lineup, but Tommy Edman has replaced him well and will play center field on Thursday. Freddie Freeman moves up a couple of spots into the No. 2 hole, followed by right fielder Kyle Tucker, who will bat third.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez takes over the cleanup spot, followed by Muncy, who slides back into third base and bats fifth. De Paula serves as the designated hitter and will bat sixth, with catcher Hunter Feduccia giving Will Smith an off day in the No. 7 spot.
Second baseman Alex Freeland will bat eight for the Dodgers, with Miguel Rojas rounding out the lineup and playing shortstop—giving Mookie Betts a well-deserved rest day.
Dodgers Lineup vs. Reds
1. Tommy Edman, CF
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Kyle Tucker, RF
4. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
5. Max Muncy, 3B
6. Josue De Paula, DH
7. Hunter Feduccia, C
8. Alex Freeland, 2B
9. Miguel Rojas, SS
P. Justin Wrobleski, LHP
Who is Starting for the Reds?
Veteran right-hander Brady Singer is starting for the Reds, making his 30th appearance of the season. He has reached that mark in each of the last three seasons, and has 25 or more appearances in all seven of his MLB campaigns bar 2020.
He isn’t having the best year despite his regular consistency, though, as he has a 5.38 ERA through 150.2 innings with only 125 strikeouts on the season.
Singer didn’t face the Dodgers in last week’s series in Los Angeles, but he has a pretty good track record against the team. In three appearances against LA, all of which came during his time with Kansas City, he has a 1.89 ERA through 19 innings with 15 strikeouts.
The Dodgers will hope to break that trend on Thursday as they look to bring themselves even closer to a first-round postseason bye. The first pitch of Thursday’s game comes at 9:40 p.m. PT.

item.content:encoded:
This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more. If you want to be featured in his new mailbag, please email newsletters@si.com with any questions about MLB or his decades in the sport.
📺 Breakdown of the Week
One of the many fascinating revelations Tarik Skubal shared with me for our upcoming SI cover piece was how he puts his entire trust in his catcher when it comes to pitch selection. That approach becomes more interesting when you change teams midseason. Skubal had more catchers in his first seven starts with the Dodgers (Hunter Feduccia, Ben Rortvedt and Will Smith) than he did in his previous 70 starts with the Tigers (Dillon Dingler and Jake Rogers).
A pattern has emerged in how the Dodgers’ catchers call pitches for Skubal as compared to the Tigers’ choices: he is leaning more into his changeup (his best pitch) and backing off his sinker (his fourth best pitch). He threw more changeups in his first month with Los Angeles (179) than he did in any month in his career. As the following chart shows, his use of his changeup has risen from 25.1% to 28.8%.
Skubal’s tweak to his arsenal as a Dodger is even more interesting when you dive into what he throws when he’s in trouble. With the Tigers, Skubal threw his four-seamer more than any other pitch with runners in scoring position (37%). With the Dodgers, the changeup has been his No. 1 choice with RISP (36%).
Skubal Pitch Choice with RISP, 2026
| Pitch Type | Tigers | Dodgers | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Four-seam fastball | 37% | 33% | -4% |
| Changeup | 29% | 36% | +7% |
| Slider | 14% | 14% | - |
| Sinker | 20% | 14% | -6% |
| Curveball | 1% | 3% | +2% |
Like the Rays, the Dodgers believe in leaning into your best pitch, especially in tight spots. How good is Skubal’s changeup? It has the highest whiff rate of any changeup in MLB (46.8%). It also is among the very best at getting out of jams:
Lowest Avg Allowed on Changeups with RISP, 2026 (Min. 125 pitches)
| Pitcher | No. of Changeups | BA |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Bradgley Rodriguez, Padres | 162 | .108 |
| 2. Tarik Skubal, Doders | 121 | .128 |
| 3. Martin Perez, Braves | 186 | .132 |
| 4. Eduardo Rodriguez, D-Backs | 174 | .133 |
📺 TV on TV This Week
Thursday, Sept. 17: Phillies at Mets, 7:15 p.m. ET (Fox)
Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor arrived in the big leagues in 2015 as a premier defender with questions about how much pop he had in his bat. Across 416 minor league games he hit just 23 home runs and slugged .387.
Eleven years later, Lindor is one of the greatest power hitting shortstops in the history of the game who is on the Hall of Fame highway. His career slugging in the majors is .472, behind only Joe Cronin (.475) among shortstops with at least 1,500 games at the position.
His next home run will be career No. 300. He will become only the 27th player with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, but the first with 1,500 games at shortstop.
Lindor has hit 292 of his home runs while playing shortstop, tying him with Miguel Tejada for third on the all-time list and within range of passing Alex Rodriguez (344) and Cal Ripken Jr. (346) to become the all-time home run leader while playing shortstop.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.content:encoded:
How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

item.content:encoded:
Teoscar Hernández volvió a demostrar que atraviesa un momento ofensivo importante y encabezó la ofensiva de los Dodgers en la victoria 4-0 sobre los Reds este martes en el Great American Ball Park.
El dominicano conectó un cuadrangular de dos carreras en la tercera entrada, su segundo vuelacercas en igual cantidad de partidos, para ampliar una ventaja que Los Ángeles ya no perdería.
Hernández terminó de 3-1 y produjo dos carreras, mientras los Dodgers se acercaron a solo dos victorias de asegurar el título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional.
El jonrón tuvo además un significado particular para Hernández, quien había tenido dificultades frente a los lanzadores derechos durante buena parte de la temporada. Hasta finales de agosto, registraba apenas .668 de OPS contra derechos, situación que incluso llevó al manager Dave Roberts a considerar un posible pelotón en el jardín izquierdo con jugadores recién ascendidos.
Después de conectar un jonrón ante el zurdo Framber Valdez en Detroit, Hernández trabajó con los coaches de bateo antes de la serie contra los Cardinals, y desde entonces su producción ha comenzado a cambiar.
Yamamoto intransitable
La actuación del dominicano sirvió como complemento perfecto para otra extraordinaria presentación de Yoshinobu Yamamoto. El japonés tuvo un comienzo poco habitual, al fallar ocho de sus primeros nueve lanzamientos y conceder boletos consecutivos a los dos primeros bateadores de Cincinnati. Fue apenas la cuarta ocasión esta temporada en que otorgó múltiples boletos en una entrada y la primera vez en su carrera de Grandes Ligas que abrió una salida con dos bases por bolas consecutivas.
Pero aquel descontrol inicial quedó rápidamente en el pasado. Después de poner a dos corredores en las bases en el primer episodio, Yamamoto solo permitió que otro bateador de Cincinnati llegara a salvo durante el resto de su actuación. Retiró a 21 de los últimos 22 bateadores que enfrentó y completó siete entradas en blanco, con apenas un hit permitido, un doble de Elly De La Cruz en el tercer inning, además de siete ponches.
La ofensiva angelina había tomado ventaja desde el segundo episodio, cuando Hunter Feduccia produjo una carrera con un sencillo. En el tercero llegó el batazo de Hernández para colocar el marcador 3-0 y, posteriormente, Alex Freeland agregó otro cuadrangular solitario para completar las cuatro carreras de Los Ángeles. El ataque de los Dodgers no fue especialmente abundante, pero produjo lo suficiente para respaldar a Yamamoto y convertir su actuación en una nueva joya monticular.
Para Yamamoto, fue además su tercera apertura consecutiva completando siete entradas y la quinta salida seguida en la que alcanzó al menos el séptimo episodio. Desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas, el derecho japonés ha mantenido un ritmo dominante, con efectividad de 1.98 en 68? entradas, 72 ponches y solo 16 boletos en 10 aperturas, una producción que lo coloca como una de las principales piezas de la rotación de Los Ángeles de cara a octubre.
La victoria dejó a los Dodgers con el número mágico en dos para conquistar su decimotercer título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional en las últimas 14 temporadas.
- Después de haber asegurado ya su boleto a la postemporada, Los Ángeles continúa ahora en busca de la corona divisional y de una posición privilegiada para octubre.
Blake Snell será el encargado de subir al montículo en el próximo encuentro de la serie, mientras los Dodgers siguen construyendo una rotación que, con Yamamoto al frente, vuelve a tomar protagonismo en su búsqueda de un tercer campeonato consecutivo.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — The Dodgers can only hope it looks this good in October.
One night after Tarik Skubal went seven innings in his first scoreless outing as a Dodger, Yoshinobu Yamamoto matched him, allowing only one hit in his seven scoreless innings as the Dodgers shut out the Cincinnati Reds, 4-0, on Tuesday night.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going tomorrow – you feel good about preventing runs,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
The win moved the Dodgers (92-59) within one day of clinching their 13th NL West division title in the past 14 seasons. Their magic number is one after the second-place San Diego Padres (82-69) lost to the Colorado Rockies later Tuesday night.
The Dodgers’ lead over the Atlanta Braves (89-63) for the No. 2 seed in the National League remains 3½ games. Their magic number to clinch a first-round bye is eight.
All of that makes the final two weeks of the regular season a chance for the Dodgers to get things right for October and their three-peat pursuit. The starting rotation appears to be there already.
Skubal has a 1.73 ERA over his past four starts. With Tuesday’s outing, Yamamoto’s ERA is 1.79 over his past seven starts. Blake Snell starts on Wednesday – and he has given up a total of only four runs in six starts since returning from elbow surgery. Only fourth starter Tyler Glasnow (eight runs in 10 innings over his past two starts) seems to have some work to do before being October-ready.
“Yeah, pretty good,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said after his first three-hit game since Aug. 17. “You have Blake Snell going tomorrow. Tyler on the back end of that too. Roki’s on his way back.
“It’s a special pitching staff. It really is. So as an offense, we just need to score a few runs for them, just like we did last year.”
Yamamoto started Tuesday by giving the Reds hope – he walked the first two batters he faced – then he took it away, retiring 21 of the next 22 batters he faced.
“They took a little moment for me,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter of the mound visit from catcher Hunter Feduccia and pitching coach Mark Prior that followed the walks. “They came up to me and, ‘Hey, how you doing?’ and just checked in on me. And then I was able to get back to my normal rhythm.”
Elly De La Cruz had the only hit off Yamamoto, a double into the left-field corner with two outs in the third inning.
But even that was a victory – Yamamoto kept him in the ballpark after De La Cruz had hit a home run in each of the previous four games between the Dodgers and Reds. He then retired the next 13 batters in order, getting six of his seven strikeouts.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine. Not giving these guys too much credit. And yeah, at first, it didn’t look promising as far as pitch count, the two walks. But then he kind of dialed things in, like he’s been known to do.”
The Dodgers gave him a lead in the second inning when Max Muncy was hit by a pitch and Tommy Edman and Hunter Feduccia followed with singles. They added to it in the third inning with a two-run home run from Teoscar Hernandez, who remains hot – 24 for 63 (.381) in his past 18 games.
“It’s been very helpful,” Roberts said of Hernandez’s late-season renaissance. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. The last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him. The defense ticked up. The at-bat quality, the taking walks, all of it. I can’t say enough about what he’s done the last 10 days.”
De La Cruz had another hit, a single in the ninth inning that put runners on the corners for the Reds with no outs. Tanner Scott struck out Sal Stewart, Jose Trevino and Eugenio Suarez to close out the shutout.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– There’s not much the Dodgers can do, manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday afternoon, to get their all-important rotation ready for the added workload that will come in the postseason.
Over the final couple weeks of the regular season, they have to just keep running their starters out there, and counting on them to round into elevated October form.
That’s what appeared to happen with Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Tuesday night at Great American Ball Park, in what was the right-hander’s most dominant performance of at least the last couple months.
In the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, Yamamoto threw a one-hit masterpiece over seven scoreless innings, flashing the kind of ruthless efficiency that defined his heroics during last year’s playoffs.
After walking his first two batters in the first inning, he retired 21 of the 22 after with seven strikeouts and virtually no stress.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine.”
The reigning World Series MVP hadn’t exactly been struggling lately, of course. Just last week, he held the Reds to one run over seven innings with 10 strikeouts back in Los Angeles.
But what Yamamoto did on Tuesday was different, keyed by quick and easy outs on soft and harmless contact.
It’s what he did as the ace of last year’s postseason staff, and what he will need to do again as the Dodgers go for a World Series three-peat this fall.
“I’d like to carry this,” Yamamoto said through an interpreter of his renewed stuff, “into October.”
The Dodgers are hoping they won’t have to ask as much out of Yamamoto this time around; that they need him to pitch back-to-back complete games (like he did in Game 2 of the NLCS and Game 2 of the World Series) or provide back-to-back nights of season-saving heroics (following up a victorious Game 6 start in the Fall Classic with a winning three-inning appearance out of the bullpen in Game 7).
But in a postseason environment, it’s impossible to know what exactly will be required.
“You can’t just try to create that during the regular season because you want these guys as strong and healthy for the October run [as possible],” Roberts said pregame. “But it’s one of those things that, once we get to the postseason, all bets are off and everyone is going to do what they can to contribute.”
It would help, of course, if the Dodgers’ currently Shohei Ohtani-less offense can keep turning a corner, with Tuesday bringing more positive –– albeit subtle –– signs.
The biggest development: Freddie Freeman returned to the lineup amid his ongoing right knee injury, and finally snapped out of a 3-for-30 slump by collecting three singles in the first, fifth and seventh innings.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday,” Roberts said, after Freeman missed his third game in the last week on Monday, “which is a good thing.”
The Dodgers’ scoring, meanwhile, came from elsewhere.

Hunter Feduccia laced an RBI single in the second off Reds starter Rhett Lowder, maintaining his unexpected status as the Dodgers’ best hitter against right-handed pitching since being re-acquired at the trade deadline (with a team-leading .292 average in such splits since the start of August).
Teoscar Hernández continued his late-season surge with a two-run homer in the third, giving him four home runs, eight extra-base hits, 18 RBIs and a .417 average over his last 14 games.
Even Alex Freeland chipped in with a solo blast in the seventh and a double in the ninth, helping him outshine fellow rookie Josue De Paula (who went 0-for-5 with his first two strikeouts of the season after getting bumped up to the leadoff spot).
That was all enough to help the team lower its magic number to clinch the National League West to one.
Still, when it comes to October, no position group will be more important than the Dodgers’ rotation.
That’s why, right now, outings like the one Yamamoto made on Tuesday, or Tarik Skubal spun the night before (also seven scoreless innings) are the most promising ways the Dodgers can ramp up toward the playoffs.
Once they get there, they’ll need their starters to be on.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– Every day, Tarik Skubal learns something new about playing for the Dodgers.
Monday's lesson: Clinching a playoff spot warrants only subtle celebrations.
"It's different than anything I've experienced, for sure," Skubal chuckled on Monday night, after the Dodgers recognized their 14th consecutive postseason berth with only a subdued postgame champagne toast and brief speech from manager Dave Roberts.
"But," the club's new star pitcher added, "I think it just speaks to the people in this room and what they expect out of this team. That was cool. A little toast and move on. Forget it happened. We've got more to accomplish this season."
Consider it the latest step in Skubal's acclimation process with the Dodgers –– another little moment that made him feel more at home with his new team.
He's now six weeks on from his emotional trade from the Detroit Tigers at the deadline.
And he's starting to find a comfort level that, after an uneven start to his Dodgers tenure, is helping him look more like the star pitcher he is accustomed to being.
"Constantly learning each other and developing relationships –– a lot of that stuff you don't realize, no one writes about that kind of relationship –– but I think it matters, it matters a lot. I probably underestimated that a little bit," said Skubal, who had spent the entirety of his career in Detroit before his marquee move to the Dodgers.
"But just communicating, having an open dialogue with everyone, all these guys, on what I like to do, what I'm comfortable with and honestly what I'm uncomfortable with … I think we're developing a real good relationship," he added.
And as a result, as manager Dave Roberts noted, "I think the last couple [outings he has made] have been his best."
That was certainly true on Monday, when Skubal spun a gem with the Dodgers' postseason berth in the balance.
He delivered his first scoreless start with the team by blanking the Reds over seven innings at Great American Ball Park. He gave up just three hits and one walk while striking out nine batters in a 90-pitch domination.
"To take the mound on the night that we had a chance to clinch, and we did it," Roberts said, "I think that's something he should be proud of."
More important to Skubal was the way it reflected his growing familiarity with the Dodgers' catchers and pitching department.
He noted he only shook Will Smith off one time all night. He praised the rhythm he has developed with pitching coaches in pre-game prep meetings. And he credited it all with helping him eliminate some perfectionist tendencies that hampered his first month with the team (when he gave up nine runs in 24 innings while lacking the ruthless efficiency that made him a reigning back-to-back Cy Young Award winner).
"I think a lot of the struggles have been 'me vs. me,' thinking too much out there and not competing the way I know how to compete," Skubal said. "Sometimes I try to be too perfect with things instead of just attacking guys over the middle of the plate and letting my stuff play, especially early in games, behind in the count, just not trying to be too fine."
To put it more simply, Skubal added, it was a process of "trying to find the rhythm of who I know I am."
And to people around the team, it's no coincidence that has happened as he's carved out a place in his new clubhouse, as well.
"He's just chill," pitching coach Mark Prior said. "You can joke around with him. You can talk to him."
Few players have grown closer with Skubal than Blake Snell to this point. They've sat side-by-side in the dugout during games, locked in constant conversation. They were pulling practical jokes on one another Tuesday, knocking over each other's chairs in the clubhouse. They've even begun making Step Brothers-inspired jokes about being new best friends on social media.
"I think we're best friends," Snell deadpanned. "Some days, he agrees."
Snell told the California Post that their relationship blossomed naturally, with Snell immediately being struck by how Skubal was "very confident and very secure with who he is" even amid new surroundings.
Two other observations:
"I didn't think he was that funny," Snell joked, describing a side of Skubal that came out Monday night when he razzed backup catcher Hunter Feduccia about a snazzy short-sleeve dress shirt and matching pair of brown slacks ("Outfit of the day!" Skubal declared).
"And," Snell added, "I like how competitive he is. Because it just makes both of us so much better."
That latter dynamic could fuel the Dodgers' entire rotation moving forward, especially entering a postseason in which the group will likely have to carry the team.
"Every time one of our boys go, we want them to dominate, and then the next man up wants to do even better," Snell said. "I think that's very important, to know that we're supporting each other and we're pushing each other to be great, and that we're not focused on just our own achievements. We're focused on our group of starting pitchers all succeeding."
Prior echoed those sentiments, noting that with Skubal specifically: "He wants to have fun. And he wants to win."
Lately, Skubal has been, now on a four-start stretch with only five runs allowed in his last 26 innings.
For the Dodgers, it's a sign of his growth process since being acquired by the club; one that could prove crucial in their three-peat ambitions.
"It's hard to get in that rhythm [and develop] that trust," Roberts said. "But for me, I see just more of the trust in whatever is called, and then you can just go out there [be himself]."

item.content:encoded:
Elly De La Cruz is truly ascending into Tungsten Arm O'Doyle territory of late.
Monday night saw him completely destroy a baseball, one that was conservatively estimated at 457 feet as it buzzed past the power stacks in left-center field in Great American Ball Park en route to exiting the stadium altogether. It was reminiscent of the superblast he hit from the other side of the plate off Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal just a week ago, feats of strength irreplicable by just about any other sole on the planet.
The Cincinnati Reds lost last night, though. Elly's homer was their lone run in a 4-1 loss to those very same Dodgers, a loss that officially eliminated the Reds from any miracle chance at a spot in the postseason. It also sunk them to 10 full games under .500 at 70-80, and this season is rapidly deteriorating into yet another one to forget and chuck onto the scrap-heap of memories of this once proud franchise.
I digress.
Rhett Lowder has a lot to improve upon as he heads into a vital offseason for his overall development. Anything short of a rapid change of form means the Reds need to build in even more redundancy in their starting depth plans for 2027, and there's been precious little in the way of advancement from their former 1st round pick so far in his own disappointing 2026. He'll get the start tonight, while the Dodgers will counter with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
First pitch in GABP is set for 6:40 PM ET. Here's how both teams will line up:
